subject: R function ':' has arguments that cannot be evaluated;

messages.author: 8df77a1c1b1da14e
messages.subject: R function ':' has arguments that cannot be evaluated;
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to specify a CAR model for segment occupancy (spatially arranged subsamples) within sample units (grid cells) where the number of segments/cell is variable. The relevant code looks like this:

  alpha1[i,1:nsegs[i]] ~ dcar_normal(adj[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]], weights[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]],num[i,1:nsegs[i]], tau1,zero_mean=1)
  weights[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]] <- 1
  # some derivations
  thetahat[i]<-mean(theta[i,1:nsegs[i]])
  meanUse[i]<- mean(u[i,1:nsegs[i]])

This means that sum_neighbors is a dynamic index (and "nsegs"). When I included sum_neighbors in constants, I got an error message:

Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames,  :
  getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse: dynamic indexing of constants is not allowed in sum_neighbors[i]. Try adding the dynamically-indexed constant as data instead (using the data argument of nimbleModel).

As advised, I instead entered it into the model as data. Then I got an error suggesting that sum_neighbors needs to be included in constants!

Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames,  :
  R function ':' has arguments that cannot be evaluated; either the function must be a nimbleFunction or values for the following inputs must be specified as constants in the model: .USED_IN_INDEX(i),.sum_neighbors_unknownIndex_sum_neighbors_oBi_cB_context2[.DYN_INDEXED(i)].

That seems like I am between a rock and a hard place, except for the suggestion to define a nimbleFunction. So I gave that a try, something like this:

CAR_prior <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(adj = double(2), sum_neighbors = double(1),num=double(2),nsegs=double(1),
     tau1=double(0)) { # type declarations
  prior ~ dcar_normal(adj[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]], weights[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]],
    num[i,1:nsegs[i]], tau1,zero_mean=1) # Site level random effects
        return(prior)
        returnType(double(2))  # return type declaration
    } )
....
meanFunc <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(X = double(1),nsegs=double(1),i=double(0)) { # type declarations
  mn <- mean(X[i,1:nsegs[i]])
        return(mn)
        returnType(double(0))  # return type declaration
    } )
....
  alpha1[i,1:nsegs[i]] <- CAR_prior(adj,sum_neighbors,num,nsegs,tau1)
  # some derivations
   thetahat[i]<-meanFunc(theta[i,1:nsegs[i]],nsegs)
  meanUse[i]<- meanFunc(u[i,1:nsegs[i]],nsegs,i=i)


But there were a few issues. First, specifying the function produced a warning about an R function (presumable it is colon operator again):

Warning message:
Detected possible use of R functions in nimbleFunction run code. For this nimbleFunction to compile, these objects must be defined as nimbleFunctions, nimbleFunctionLists, or nimbleLists: ~.

And then when I tried to use the functions anyway, I still got the Error about the R function arguments that can't be evaluated, this time apparently in refence to "nsegs".

There may be deeper issues with my model, but I guess my question for now is this:
Is it possible to use a colon indexing operator when the upper limit specifies a dynamic index (in my call to dcar_normal)?
Is it the colon itself that must be defined as a nimbleFunction?

Thanks,
Glenn

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: R function ':' has arguments that cannot be evaluated;
parts:
Glenn, thanks so much for your use and interest in NIMBLE, in particular your use of the CAR spatial models.  Let's get this figured out.

Definitely no need to define the colon (" : ") operator as a nimbleFunction, but good on you for considering that.

I feel like what you're trying to do should work fine.  To be clear, I don't believe that in your model sum_neighbors (nor nsegs) is dynamically indexed.  That would imply that the *indexing used for sum_neighbors[]* (same goes for nsegs), itself, is a dynamically-valued node in the model.  In this case, in your model, that index is "i", which I'm guessing is a loop-index (e.g. for(i in 1:N), { .... sum_neighbors[i] .... }.  In the dynamically indexed case, it would rather appear as: i ~ dSomeDistribution(...)

Again, I'm guessing that your use of the index "i" is not a dynamic index, and thus sum_neighbors (nor nsegs) is not dynamically indexed in your model, and therefore you should be fine providing both sum_neighbors and nsegs in as "constants" to the model, as you tried.  So like I said at the beginning, I think what you're trying to do should work fine.

All that said, I can't actually see what's going on, with just the minimal code snippets you provided.  I'm not asking you to share your full model on this public list, nor to share it directly with me.  But if you want us to take a look, we'll need some sort of reproducible example of the problem you're having, so we can figure it out.

Hope this helps!  Keep in touch.

Daniel

parts:
Agreed that we'll need a reproducible example.

If I follow your message, Glenn, you tried changing how sum_neighbors is provided (data vs. constants).

What about nsegs?  To be sure: It can't be a stochastic node since it appears as an index on the left-hand side of a declaration.

Let's not get into your attempt to write a nimbleFunction.  A nimbleFunction does not hold model declarations, so your use of "~" wouldn't work there.  We should be able to work this out within the model code.

-Perry

parts:
Thanks for the quick replies - I have attached an example (which I am not entirely sure is correct). And apologies in advance for the following long post. But I've been trying to do some additional sleuthing, and try here to explain what I have found (or not).


The one piece I’m not sure I mentioned is that some of the cells have only a single segment, so no neighborhood can be defined for those cells. So I used double indexing accounting like Daniel described here (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/hJejjex5C_4 ), where I tried to define a CAR prior for alpha1 in the cases where there were >1 segments, and set alpha1==0 otherwise. That seems to be a problem, because when I drop out that complication and make sure all cells have >2 segments (example also included), then the dynamic indexing error goes away (with nsegs and sum_neighbors included in constants rather than data; including them in data still generates the error about R function arguments than can't be evaluated). However, I did still get a bunch of warnings about NaNs that are produced when I run "nimMC$run(1)", and also another, different error, at the compilation step (of the model).


Cnim <- compileNimble(nim)
Error: Failed to create the shared library

Not sure what is the issue with the NaNs produced, but based on this post (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/a693revKUMM), I thought there might be a type mismatch problem in the compilation. It looks there might be an issue with weights, and indeed, supplying weights as constants eliminated that compilation error. However, there is still the problem with the NaNs, and also at the second compilation step, there is an additional error (sometimes)


CnimMC <- compileNimble(nimMC,project=nim)
Error in `*tmp*`[[jj]] :
  attempt to select less than one element in integerOneIndex

I wasn't able to figure out anything from looking at the compiler output, but curiously, when I just simply tried it again a second time (just repeated "CnimMC <- compileNimble(nimMC,project=nim)"), it did not produce the error (but seemed to compile suspiciously quickly). And it clearly is not correct, because a call to runMCMC failed. Calling the uncompiled mcmc object didn't fail to run, but predictably produced the same NaN warnings.


All that trial and error above was for the case where all cells have >2 segments. I suspect I might have a silly error somewhere and just can't seem to see it. But I also don't have a lot of experience with spatial models and so am not sure if I am trying to do something ill-advised.


Regarding the scenario where some cells do have only a single segment, there may be a few other issues.

First, when nsegs[i] evaluates to 1, then my model has, in two places, index ranges that evaluate to something like "for(seg in 1:1), or mean(theta[i,1:1]). I'm not sure if such indexing is allowed.


Second, of course, if number of segments is generated randomly (as in a simulation), than the model is completely inappropriate if by chance all of the cells have >1 segment. In that case, I think it would be easy to have a switch to use another model. What is less clear to me is if the model should work if only one cell has a single segment. I think maybe it would fail in that case as well (at the compilations step) because then the index vector for the cells than have only 1 segment (no_neighbors) would be of length 1, and the attempt to index it with no_neighbors[ind] would be problematic (a type mismatch again). If so, I could probably again write a clever switch to deal with such a case. But at this point, I can't get past the dynamic indexing issue.


Thanks,

Glenn

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: R function ':' has arguments that cannot be evaluated;
parts:
Glenn, I've made a lot of progress with your model, and fixed a number of problems.  I'll encourage you to carefully look through the attached script (sandbox_DT.R), with particular attention to the comments I've added which begin with "DT: ...", where I've added some helpful or explanatory comments.

That said, I wasn't able to completely fix the first model, as there's a problem with your generation of the adjacency matrix, and I'm not sure what the intent of your code was exactly, but I am sure it's not doing what you're intended.  Specifically, in the case where nsegs = 2, which happens in your example when ind=15, the function you wrote getAdjMatrix() to generate the adj matrix, I don't believe it's functioning correctly in that case of nsegs = 2.

In that case, then loop for (i in 2:(nsegs[j] - 1)) { ends up doing some "backwards indexing", where the loop indexing constant i take the value of 2, then decrements to take the value of 1.  In this situation, as written, that line of the adjacency matrix (adj[15, ]) ends up having  a "0" in the first position, that is, adj[15, 1] = 0, which cannot be as intended, as it suggests that cell number 15 is a neighbor with cell number 0, which doesn't exist.

This then leads to a new problem in the use of the dcar_normal() distribution, since it has issues with this 0.

That said, I fixed a lot of other problems (in the attached script), so many so that there's a reasonable (well, at least non-zero) chance that if you fix up this issue with the generation of the adj matrix (in the function getAdjMatrix() ), then the first example in this script might just work.

The big issue I'll mention, for you, and for anyone else reading this, was that the BUGS modelling language is *declarative*, that is, every line, or each time a line in a for loop is executed, should declare a *new node*, and not try to define any sort of "intermediate temporary variable".  This was causing a problem (previously) in your lines of model code that looked like:

for(ind in ....) {
    i <- .....
    alpha1[ .... various uses of the i variable ...]
}

Further, interestingly, I was not able to re-create the compilation issue that you had in the second example.  It compiled fine for me.  That said, I don't believe the *model* in the second example was fully well-formed, since model$calculate() returned NA, which generally indicates a problem of some sort.  But I figured at least starting with correcting all the things I've pointed out, will be a good start in updating the second model, as well.

There's a good place to start.  Please keep in touch if you still have issues, once you fix up the adj matrix, and the other things I've pointed out in the attached script.

Cheers!
Daniel

The big issue I'll mention, for you, and for anyone else reading this, was that the BUGS modelling language is *declarative*, that is, every line, or each time a line in a for loop is executed, should declare a *new node*, and not try to define any sort of "intermediate temporary variable".  This was causing a problem (previously) in your lines of model code that looked like:

for(ind in ....) {
    i <- .....
    alpha1[ .... various uses of the i variable ...]
}

Further, interestingly, I was not able to re-create the compilation issue that you had in the second example.  It compiled fine for me.  That said, I don't believe the *model* in the second example was fully well-formed, since model$calculate() returned NA, which generally indicates a problem of some sort.  But I figured at least starting with correcting all the things I've pointed out, will be a good start in updating the second model, as well.

There's a good place to start.  Please keep in touch if you still have issues, once you fix up the adj matrix, and the other things I've pointed out in the attached script.

Cheers!
Daniel
On Mon, Feb 11, 2019 at 2:50 PM Glenn Stauffer <gesta...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thanks for the quick replies - I have attached an example (which I am not entirely sure is correct). And apologies in advance for the following long post. But I've been trying to do some additional sleuthing, and try here to explain what I have found (or not).


The one piece I’m not sure I mentioned is that some of the cells have only a single segment, so no neighborhood can be defined for those cells. So I used double indexing accounting like Daniel described here (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/hJejjex5C_4 ), where I tried to define a CAR prior for alpha1 in the cases where there were >1 segments, and set alpha1==0 otherwise. That seems to be a problem, because when I drop out that complication and make sure all cells have >2 segments (example also included), then the dynamic indexing error goes away (with nsegs and sum_neighbors included in constants rather than data; including them in data still generates the error about R function arguments than can't be evaluated). However, I did still get a bunch of warnings about NaNs that are produced when I run "nimMC$run(1)", and also another, different error, at the compilation step (of the model).


Cnim <- compileNimble(nim)
Error: Failed to create the shared library

Not sure what is the issue with the NaNs produced, but based on this post (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/a693revKUMM), I thought there might be a type mismatch problem in the compilation. It looks there might be an issue with weights, and indeed, supplying weights as constants eliminated that compilation error. However, there is still the problem with the NaNs, and also at the second compilation step, there is an additional error (sometimes)


CnimMC <- compileNimble(nimMC,project=nim)
Error in `*tmp*`[[jj]] :
  attempt to select less than one element in integerOneIndex

I wasn't able to figure out anything from looking at the compiler output, but curiously, when I just simply tried it again a second time (just repeated "CnimMC <- compileNimble(nimMC,project=nim)"), it did not produce the error (but seemed to compile suspiciously quickly). And it clearly is not correct, because a call to runMCMC failed. Calling the uncompiled mcmc object didn't fail to run, but predictably produced the same NaN warnings.


All that trial and error above was for the case where all cells have >2 segments. I suspect I might have a silly error somewhere and just can't seem to see it. But I also don't have a lot of experience with spatial models and so am not sure if I am trying to do something ill-advised.


Regarding the scenario where some cells do have only a single segment, there may be a few other issues.

First, when nsegs[i] evaluates to 1, then my model has, in two places, index ranges that evaluate to something like "for(seg in 1:1), or mean(theta[i,1:1]). I'm not sure if such indexing is allowed.


Second, of course, if number of segments is generated randomly (as in a simulation), than the model is completely inappropriate if by chance all of the cells have >1 segment. In that case, I think it would be easy to have a switch to use another model. What is less clear to me is if the model should work if only one cell has a single segment. I think maybe it would fail in that case as well (at the compilations step) because then the index vector for the cells than have only 1 segment (no_neighbors) would be of length 1, and the attempt to index it with no_neighbors[ind] would be problematic (a type mismatch again). If so, I could probably again write a clever switch to deal with such a case. But at this point, I can't get past the dynamic indexing issue.


Thanks,

Glenn

Thanks Glenn.

Regarding C++ compiler warnings: Due to the variety of compilers on different systems and the fact that different compilers emit warnings for different code situations and accept different compiler flags, it is difficult to make every compiler completely happy.  As a result, we accept that compilers will issue warnings, and typically the C++ compiler output is not shown in the R session.  So, you are correct: as long as there are no compiler errors, it should be ok.

-Perry
